Learning Objectives
Assess the biopsychosocial variables contributing to low back pain.
Address the importance, relevance, and interpretation of red flags in the evaluation of low
back pain.
Interpret the value of active treatment and exercise, particularly in patients with low back pain.
Compare the value and application of injections in patients with a spinal disorder.
Assess the role of electrodiagnostic studies in patients with a spinal disorder.
Establish indications for cognitive behavioral treatment strategies in patients with a spinal
disorder.

Low back pain (LBP) is very common.
True pathologic diagnosis of LBP often is uncertain.
Most painful episodes of LBP are self-limiting, particularly those associated with axial pain.

Introduction
This lesson will broadly review the nonsurgical management of degenerative spine
disorders. In general, patients more commonly seek treatment for lumbar spine
conditions rather than cervical spine conditions. In addition, data on the efficacy of
management of lumbar spine conditions are more abundant and of higher quality than
data on the efficacy of management of cervical spine conditions. This lesson primarily
focuses on management of the lumbar spine, particularly lumbar spine conditions that
result in axial pain. Many of the concepts and outcomes in this lesson can be
extrapolated to other aspects of nonsurgical spine management.
LBP is the most common reason patients seek treatment for the spine. LBP is not a
diagnosis but a symptom; however, true pathologic diagnosis beyond degenerative spine
disease often remains elusive. Recent data suggest a mean point prevalence of LBP of
18% worldwide; however, the prevalence of LBP is higher (median, 30%) in high-income
countries. Risk factors for LBP include the amount and frequency of lifting; smoking;
obesity; and psychosocial factors, particularly depression. LBP is the leading cause of
years lived with disability and the leading chronic health problem forcing workers to
retire. In 1996, estimated indirect costs associated with LBP in the United States ranged
from $18 billion to $28 billion.1
Often, symptoms resulting from spinal disorders are self-limiting. Most patients respond
favorably to observation and nonsurgical treatment. This is particularly true for patients
with conditions causing isolated axial pain.
Electrodiagnostic Studies
Electrodiagnostic studies are used to evaluate a problem with the nerves, muscles, or both.

9/3/26, 5:24 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049

Most commonly, this evaluation is done via electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction
studies (NCS). Locations evaluated include the anterior horn cell, nerve root, peripheral nerve,
neuromuscular junction, and muscle.
Electrodiagnostic studies do not have a role in the evaluation of patients with axial symptoms
alone.
Electrodiagnostic studies may not detect abnormalities for up to 3 weeks after axonal injury.

Electrodiagnostic Studies
Electrodiagnostic studies may help localize muscle or nerve disorders and may help
differentiate neurologic complaints that are spinal in origin from those that are
extraspinal in origin. Electrodiagnostic studies do not provide information in the
evaluation of axial pain. In patients with radiculopathy, NCS will be normal. EMG studies
will be abnormal in two separate muscles sharing the same nerve root but innervated by
different peripheral nerves. In patients with myelopathy, NCS will be normal. EMG
studies often will be normal; however, fasciculations and polyradiculopathy, which
suggest myelopathy, may be noted. In patients with an acute condition, EMG studies
may be normal for up to 3 weeks postinjury.
Nerve Conduction Studies
NCS involve surface electrical stimulation to test the response of a nerve. NCS can be used to
assess motor and sensory nerves (Figure 1).
NCS allow for accurate localization of a focal lesion and aid in detection of a generalized
disease process that affects conduction along accessible portions of the peripheral nerve.
Neuropraxia is the term used to describe lesions in which a conduction block is present.

9/3/26, 5:24 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049

Figure 1 Photograph of a hand shows the setup for a median motor nerve conduction study to
the abductor pollicis brevis. The ground electrode is placed on the dorsum of the hand.
(Reproduced from Colorado B, Sanders JO, Foxx K: Electrodiagnostic testing and intraoperative
neurophysiologic monitoring, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 87-101.)

Nerve Conduction Studies
NCS test the speed or conduction velocity and the qualitative action potential
morphology, including amplitude, of a nerve (Figure 2). A stimulated nerve conducts in
the intended direction (eg, from the spine to the muscle for a motor nerve; orthodromic)
and in the opposite direction (antidromic). NCS allow for accurate localization of a focal
lesion and aid in detection of a generalized disease process that affects conduction along
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
4/30

accessible portions of the peripheral nerve. Nerve conduction velocity helps differentiate
radiculopathy (normal) from peripheral nerve compression (abnormal).2
The most common NCS performed are:
Compound motor action potential: Summation of motor axons
Sensory nerve action potential: Summation of sensory axons
Mixed sensory and motor NCS
Hoffmann reflex (monosynaptic spinal reflex): Orthodromic stimulation of sensory
nerves that synapse at spinal level and return orthodromic via motor nerves; most
useful for evaluation of S1 radiculopathy.
F wave: Stimulation of the muscle that measures antidromic conduction along the
motor nerve to the spine and orthodromic return to the muscle; not as useful for
routine evaluation of radiculopathy.
Figure 2 Image shows an action potential waveform. In this example, a compound

(peak to peak), p = peak, o = onset. (Reproduced from Colorado B, Sanders JO, Foxx K:
Electrodiagnostic testing and intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring, in Truumees E,

Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 87-101.)
Electromyography
EMG studies primarily test the muscle but also provide indirect information about the nerve.
EMG studies allow for observation of intrinsic electrical activity from muscle. EMG studies
involve the use of recording needles (Figure 3).
For radiculopathy:
EMG is specific but lacks sensitivity; pain fibers are not tested during EMG.
Abnormality in two separate muscles sharing the same nerve root but innervated by
different peripheral nerves suggests radiculopathy.
For myelopathy:
EMG studies and NCS usually are normal.
EMG studies are positive only if motor neurons are affected.
Polyradicular findings also may indicate myelopathy.

Figure 3 Photograph of a hand shows the basic setup for needle electromyography. (Reproduced
from Colorado B, Sanders JO, Foxx K: Electrodiagnostic testing and intraoperative
neurophysiologic monitoring, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 87-101.)

Electromyography
Normal EMG studies should be quiet at rest. Spontaneous activity at rest may indicate
various neurologic conditions:
Sharp waves: Impaired innervation or injured muscle
Fibrillation potentials: Impaired innervation
Complex repetitive discharges: Neurogenic and myopathic disorders; tend to occur in
patients with more longstanding disorders and suggest injury older than 6 months.
EMG analyzes various features of the action potential, which may indicate normal
function and abnormal myogenic or neurogenic function.

For radiculopathy, EMG is specific but lacks sensitivity. Pain fibers are not tested during
EMG. Abnormality in two separate muscles sharing the same nerve root but innervated
by different peripheral nerves suggests radiculopathy. In patients with myelopathy, EMG
studies and NCS usually are normal. EMG studies are positive only if motor neurons are
affected. Polyradicular findings also may indicate myelopathy.
Laboratory Studies

Laboratory Studies
In general, laboratory studies are not necessary for patients with LBP. If infection,
cancer, or autoimmune disease is suspected, then surgeons should considered
obtaining a patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and
complete blood count or evaluating a patient’s stool or urine for blood. Tests suggestive
of autoimmune diseases, such as a rheumatoid factor test, antinuclear antibody test,
cyclic citrullinated peptide test, and human leukocyte antigen-B27 test, also should be
considered.
Contributions to Diagnosis
Red Flag Conditions
All patients must be screened for risk factors for red flag conditions, specifically fracture,
tumor, infection, and substantial or progressive neurologic injury (myelopathy, radiculopathy,
cauda equina).

Red Flag Conditions
In general, wide variations exist with regard to clinical guidelines on red flag conditions.
In general, some risk factors cited are poorly validated, and certain symptoms or risk
factors are associated with a high prevalence in the primary care population.3-5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
8/30

Therefore, isolated risk factors should not be an absolute indication for acute imaging
studies, and the absence of risk factors should not be an absolute contraindication to
acute imaging studies. Clinical suspicion in combination with the presence of multiple
symptoms or predictors may increase the likelihood of substantial pathology. Red flags
should be thought of as factors to consider in clinical decision making for management.
The decision to obtain imaging studies should be made in the context of planning clinical
management. A primary risk factor for cancer is a history of malignancy. Primary risk
factors for fracture include substantial trauma, minor trauma in patients with a known
or high likelihood of osteoporosis, and a visible contusion. Primary risk factors for
infection include fever, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, and corticosteroid
use.
Differential Diagnosis
Spinal structures
Systemic processes
Psychosocial factors: Nonorganic pain

Differential Diagnosis
Numerous spinal structures may cause or be associated with spinal pain. Spinal pain
may result from systemic disease processes, such as inflammatory arthropathies.
Numerous nonspinal structures, including the hip joint, musculotendinous structures,
the kidney, the gallbladder, and the esophagus, can cause referred pain or mimic spinal
pain, resulting in symptoms often associated with spinal structures. Psychosocial factors
are associated with spinal pain and are the strongest predictors of patient outcomes.
Psychosocial Considerations
Spinal pain is best thought of as a biopsychosocial problem (Resource 1).
Pain is a subjective symptom and reflective of a patient’s current and lifetime experiences.

Following a purely anatomic model for understanding spinal pain is ineffective in many
patients.
Psychosocial factors are stronger predictors of patient outcomes than anatomic or imaging
factors.

Psychosocial Considerations
Depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders, and other
mental health conditions are highly prevalent in patients with ongoing spinal pain.
Mental health conditions are present in a large proportion of individuals with chronic
pain. This relationship is bidirectional, meaning that patients with a underlying mental
health disorder have an increased risk for chronic pain and mental health disorder occur
in patients with chronic pain.6,7 Anatomic considerations may be apparent in some
patients with spinal pain, and roles for particular treatment options may be well-
identified; however, these considerations are not entirely clear in many patients. Fear
avoidance, meaning the conscious or subconscious avoidance of activity because of
excessive fear of harm, plays a larger role than pain in the disability associated with
spinal pain. In patients in whom psychological distress or other psychosocial factors are
substantial drivers of pain and disability, treatment directed at putative structural causes
of pain alone may be ineffective or harmful. In the management of pain, particularly in
patients without clear structural correlates, managing mental health issues and negative
belief structures and promoting a sense of self-efficacy are more in line with existing
data.
Anatomic Structures in Spinal Pain
All structures sharing the same segmental embryologic origin refer pain to similar locations;
therefore, substantial overlap exists between referral patterns for various structures of the
same spinal level, which often precludes differentiation via a patient history and physical
examination.
Ligamentous, musculotendinous, and other soft-tissue structures may result in locations of
pain similar to those of other spinal structures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
10/30


Anatomic Structures in Spinal Pain
In general, pain in the lumbar spine is referred to the adjacent to subjacent paraspinal to
sacral region or proximal lower extremity. In the cervical spine, discogenic pain is
referred to the subjacent paraspinal to scapular region. Zygapophyseal/facet joints may
cause pain that is referred to regions similar to those of the associated intervertebral
disk. Involvement of the nerve root at a given spinal level typically is associated with
referred dermatomal pain, neurologic loss with or without pain, or myotomal pain;
however, it is not typically associated with axial pain. Differentiation of structural causes
of axial spine pain via a physical examination alone is extremely limited and generally
does not result in validated pathognomonic findings for specific structures.
Axial Versus Radicular Pain
Differentiation of axial pain from radicular pain is critical in creating a differential diagnosis
and considering treatment options.
Axial pain may result from various local spine structures and may be difficult to differentiate.
In general, radicular pain indicates involvement of a nerve root, with symptoms following a
particular distribution in the limb.

Axial Versus Radicular Pain
Differentiation of axial syndromes from radicular syndromes is critical in the
management of lumbar spine disorders. Frequently, the etiology of axial spine pain is
nonspecific because of the substantial overlap of symptoms arising from specific
structures. The ability to differentiate between these symptoms based on a patient
history and physical examination is limited. Excluding acute medical or surgical concerns,
most treatment options for the management of axial pain do not depend on a specific
structural diagnosis. Global considerations for restoring range of motion and normal
spine function, reducing fear and anxiety, and progressing patients toward restored
function are paramount, and nonsurgical management generally is not specific to
individual spinal structures. Involvement of a nerve root substantially alters the clinical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
11/30

approach. Surgical decompression and epidural steroid injections are more effective in
the management of problems with the nerve root origin rather than causes of axial pain.
The relative consistency of dermatomal and myotomal findings and the ability to identify
focal nerve compression or pathology via imaging studies or electrodiagnostic studies
enhances the accuracy of diagnosis of radicular syndromes.
Differentiating Factors in the Patient History
Patient age: The frequency of certain spinal pathologies and injuries varies substantially by
patient age.
Biologic sex: The frequency of numerous medical conditions, including osteoporosis,
spondyloarthropathy, neck pain, and genetic disorders, varies substantially by biologic sex.
Social determinants of health are important but understudied contributors to health. Access to
health care, access to appropriate nutrition, access to a safe living environment, treatment
bias, physical and psychological comorbidities, and numerous other factors may affect
management.

Differentiating Factors in the Patient History
Spinal pain considerations vary based on individual patient factors. Adolescents tend to
have bone, inflammatory, genetic, and oncologic issues that are distinct from those that
occur in adults. Disk herniations most frequently occur in adults in their thirties through
fifties, and degenerative conditions, osteoporosis, and additional oncologic conditions
are more common in older adults. The prevalence of specific conditions varies by
biologic sex (eg, osteoporosis and neck pain are more common in women). Social
determinants of health are important but understudied contributors to health.
Experience with the healthcare system, experience with physical activity, and social and
cultural influences affect pain and health and may play a role in patient presentation and
treatment. These factors are important to consider in the initial treatment of all patients
but are particularly important to consider in patients with red flag conditions, patients
who fail to respond to initial guideline-based treatment, patients with apparent
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
12/30

inconsistencies in presentation and evaluation findings, and patients with increased
levels of distress or pain.8
Risk Stratification
Risk stratification allows for the appropriate use of psychological or multimodal approaches to
management.
Decisions regarding nonsurgical treatment are affected by a patient’s relative risk for certain
conditions and treatment outcomes.
Appropriate risk stratification is the basis for most imaging and diagnostic guidelines for spinal
pain.
Psychosocial risk factors often are termed yellow flags; these factors affect initial diagnostic
and treatment strategies and clinical outcomes.

Risk Stratification
Risk stratification allows for the appropriate use of psychological or multimodal
approaches to management. Psychosocial risk factors often are termed yellow flags;
these factors affect initial diagnostic and treatment strategies and clinical outcomes. The
appropriateness and effectiveness of specific nonsurgical treatment modalities may vary
based on the presence of specific yellow flags. Common yellow flags include widespread
pain, poor sleep, job dissatisfaction, a long period of time off work, absence of light duty
alternatives, fear avoidance, depression, anxiety, self-perceived poor health, and a
history of abuse.8 The STarT Back Screening Tool is a 9-item, self-reported screening
method used to stratify patients with LBP by psychosocial risk. Patients with LBP and
lower STarT Back scores tend to respond to relatively focused treatment via physical
therapy. Patients with LBP and higher STarT Back scores tend to require a longer course
of treatment and have better outcomes if psychological intervention is incorporated into
treatment.9 Passive treatment modalities, such as topical heat, massage, or
manipulation, may be inappropriate or counterproductive for many patients with fear
avoidance or related yellow flags.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM

Nonsurgical Management
General Considerations
Various nonsurgical treatment options are available for patients with spinal pain, most of
which are associated with little to no high-quality evidence to support their use.
The primary goals of nonsurgical management are to restore/optimize function and preserve
long-term health.

General Considerations
The primary goals of nonsurgical management are to restore/optimize function and
preserve long-term health. Although the management of pain is important, treatment
considerations should focus on a patient’s long-term health rather than short-term pain
relief, if possible. Providing advice or assistance to encourage movement/activity;
providing reassurance that an activity is safe; fostering goal-directed behavior and a
return to normal activities; and avoiding unnecessary tests, physical restrictions, and
catastrophic thinking are critical to effective nonsurgical management (Resource 1).
Medications
No medication is associated with long-term effectiveness in patients with chronic spine pain.
No high-quality evidence supports the long-term use of opioid medications to manage spinal
pain; however, opioid medications may provide modest short-term benefits of questionable
clinical importance in patients with chronic LBP.
No evidence supports the use of a particular combination of medications for the management
of LBP.

Medications
Medications are not remarkably effective across the spectrum of nonspecific spinal pain
(Resource 2). In patients with acute spinal pain, simple analgesic agents are relatively
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
14/30

ineffective. NSAIDs afford some modest benefits but may be associated with
gastrointestinal issues. Skeletal muscle relaxants provide short-term benefits but are
associated with sedative properties. Acetaminophen is ineffective in the management of
spinal pain.10,11
In general, medication studies are performed in populations of subjects with relatively
nonspecific axial or radicular pain, mostly in the lumbar spine region. Certain
medications for the management of particular structural conditions are poorly studied.
Given the overall health and function of a patient with spinal pain, the effect of certain
medical therapies in the management of particular findings noted on clinical
presentation, such as depression, sleep, anxiety, and inflammation, is not well studied.
Management of these issues may afford additional benefits. Although antidepressants in
general do not appear to be effective, duloxetine may afford modest short-term benefits
in patients with chronic spine pain. However, duloxetine is associated with a relatively
high rate of adverse effects, and the long-term effects of duloxetine have not been
studied.9 Moderate to strong evidence indicates that anticonvulsants are ineffective in
the management of LBP and radicular pain.12 No high-quality evidence supports the
long-term use of opioid medications to manage spinal pain; however, opioid medications
may provide modest short-term benefits of questionable clinical importance in patients
with chronic LBP. Opioid medications should be used judiciously given the potential
adverse effects.13 No evidence supports the use of a particular combination of
medications for the management of LBP.14
Spinal Manipulative Therapy
Low-level evidence shows that spinal manipulative therapy for the management of various
spinal pain syndromes may be associated with short- or intermediate-term benefits with
regard to pain and function; however, the magnitude of any potential benefits is small.
Spinal manipulative therapy is not associated with substantial long-term benefits.

Spinal Manipulative Therapy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
15/30

A large number of patients with spinal pain seek or initiate treatment with chiropractors
or other practitioners of spinal manipulative therapy. Despite widespread use of spinal
manipulative therapy for the management of spinal pain syndromes, insufficient
evidence shows any dramatic or long-term improvement with regard to pain or function.
Low-level evidence shows that spinal manipulative therapy for the management of
various spinal pain syndromes may be associated with short- or intermediate-term
benefits with regard to pain or function; however, the magnitude of any potential
benefits is small.15 High-level evidence shows that spinal manipulative therapy affords
no substantial benefit over other active treatment options.16
The nonspecific effects of chiropractic visits or concurrent components of treatment
have not been studied but may affect patient perceptions of benefits. A limited course of
spinal manipulative therapy is a clinical treatment option; however, extended treatment
without documented benefits is inappropriate (Resource 3).
Physical Therapy
Physical therapy encompasses a wide range of treatment options, including topical modalities,
manual therapy/mobilization, exercise, and education.
Physical therapy training includes anatomic, physiologic, kinesiologic, orthopaedic, and
neurologic examinations.

Physical Therapy
Physical therapy is highly variable and may include a diverse range of treatment
approaches. Little agreement exists with regard to the optimal care paradigm for
physical therapy in the management spinal disorders. Physical therapists may
recommend various passive treatment modalities and a wide range of exercise for a
given patient. Management of biomechanical deficits via performing stretches and
exercise, overcoming fear, educating patients about their condition, and fostering a goal-
directed approach to long-term physical activity may be the most beneficial components
of physical therapy for patients with a spinal disorder. In the US healthcare system,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
16/30

physical therapy is the standard method for providing patients with education and
training on therapeutic exercise.
Physical therapy orders should include appropriate diagnostic information, treatment
goals, and any precautions or restrictions. Physical therapy provided via a behavioral
health approach may be more effective in many patients with chronic spine pain. Active
management, particularly exercise, is more beneficial than passive management, such as
topical heat or electrical stimulation. Mechanical or manual cervical traction may be
beneficial in the management of cervical radicular pain.17 Lumbar traction is not
effective in the treatment of patients who have LBP with or without radicular
symptoms.18
Acupuncture
Studies comparing various forms of acupuncture and studies comparing acupuncture with
other active treatment options in the management spinal pain are lacking.
Several recent guidelines recommend acupuncture to treat patients with chronic LBP;
however, many studies evaluating immediate posttreatment pain have reported that the
magnitude of any potential benefit is extremely small and the duration of any potential benefit
is short.
No evidence supports the use of acupuncture to manage neuropathic pain.

Acupuncture
In 2020, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality published a systematic review
on noninvasive, nonpharmacologic management of chronic pain.15,19 The report stated
that acupuncture had a small short-term effect on chronic LBP. The report defines a
small effect as a change of 0.5 to 1.0 on a 10-point visual analog scale for pain, which is
well below the standard minimal clinically important difference on this scale and may be
within the range of the error of measurement. The level of evidence supporting this
statement is low, and the duration of any potential benefit is short. In addition, the long-
term benefits of acupuncture are not superior to those of other active treatment options
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
17/30

(Resource 4). No evidence supports the use of acupuncture to manage neuropathic
pain.20 Similar to other treatment options, acupuncture is not a uniform discipline, with
the training of and technique used by providers varying greatly.
Exercise
For patients with acute LBP, exercise is an effective treatment option; however, no evidence
shows that exercise is superior to other forms of acute treatment or that any one form of
exercise is superior to other forms of exercise.
For patients with chronic LBP, exercise affords meaningful improvements in pain and function;
however, no evidence shows that any one form of exercise is superior to other forms of
exercise.
For patients with chronic LBP, specific approaches, including core/stabilization exercises and
the McKenzie method, are not associated with unique benefits and are equivalent to other
forms of active exercise.
Exercise is associated with considerable health benefits, including decreased pain, improved
cardiovascular health, improved mental health, and preservation of function. A combination of
aerobic and resistance training offers additional benefits.

Exercise
Various therapeutic exercises, including cardiovascular exercise; resistance training;
patterns of basic movements; postural or functional exercises for a given muscle group;
and organized activities, such as yoga, Pilates, dancing, and martial arts, can be used to
manage of spinal disorders. Incorporating exercise into nonsurgical management and
postoperative management may help patients achieve long-term health and functional
changes (managing mental health also may be beneficial). This treatment approach is
distinct from various passive treatment modalities that often are used to help patients
achieve short-term pain relief. Studies have reported that exercise is consistently helpful
in the management of spinal pain. The incorporation of exercise structures that help
manage fear and coping needs into treatment is particularly helpful for patients who
struggle with such issues. Some forms of exercise, such as yoga, have been studied to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
18/30

some extent and appear to be beneficial, whereas few studies are available on other
forms of exercise, such as Pilates.
The type of exercise that a patient pursues is not as important as the fact the patient is
pursuing exercise. Much of the spine community believes that certain exercises are
critical to success and that every individual needs a strong core. These philosophies are
not supported by data, which show equivalency between multiple forms of active
exercise programs, including those that focus on core stability. The ideal exercise is one
that a patient enjoys, has access to, can afford, and is appropriate for their medical
issues. In certain patient populations, the addition of psychologically informed or
cognitive behavioral treatment strategies to an active exercise program may be critical to
improve outcomes.21 For patients with acute LBP, exercise is an effective treatment
option; however, no evidence shows that exercise is superior to other forms of acute
treatment or that any one form of exercise is superior to other forms of exercise.
Regardless, patients who remain active after acute episodes appear to have better
outcomes.19,22 For patients with chronic LBP, exercise affords meaningful improvements
in pain and function; however, no evidence shows that any one form of exercise is
superior to other forms of exercise.23 For patients with chronic LBP, specific approaches,
including core/stabilization exercises and the McKenzie method, are not associated with
unique benefits and are equivalent to other forms of active exercise.19,22 For patients
with chronic LBP, exercise in combination with cognitive behavioral treatment strategies
may be particularly helpful.19
Limited data is available on the use of exercise to manage lumbar spine stenosis or disk
herniation. Given the natural histories of these disorders, remaining engaged in exercise
is associated with benefits. Neck pain, with or without radicular pain, is studied less than
LBP. Postural/scapular stabilization exercises may be helpful.24
Behavioral/Psychological Approaches
Behavioral management can be provided by mental health professionals; however, behavioral
treatment techniques can be used by all healthcare providers and can be incorporated into
other active treatment options.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:24 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Spinal Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000049
19/30

Behavioral therapy is associated with modest short-term improvements in patients with
chronic LBP.
Behavioral therapy is particularly helpful in combination with physical therapy and active
exercise.
For patients with neck pain, limited available data suggest that psychological therapies linked
to exercise-based treatment approaches afford benefits with regard to pain and function.
Psychological factors are associated with poor treatment outcomes and a shift from acute pain
to chronic pain; such factors should be considered in the evaluation of all patients with spinal
pain.

Behavioral/Psychological Approaches
Although the management of mental health issues and psychological factors, such as
fear avoidance, is beneficial, behavioral treatment approaches generally are
underutilized in the management of spinal pain. All healthcare providers can apply
knowledge of the psychology of pain to help patients benefit from other treatment
options, the most studied of which is exercise. Incorporating goals, working through fear,
and helping patients gain confidence are psychologically based treatment strategies.
Behavioral therapy is associated with modest short-term improvements in patients with
chronic LBP.15,25 Behavioral therapy is particularly helpful in combination with physical
therapy and active exercise.19 For patients with neck pain, limited available data suggest
that psychological therapies linked to exercise-based treatment approaches afford
benefits with regard to pain and function.26
Psychological factors are associated with poor treatment outcomes and a shift from
acute pain to chronic pain; such factors should be considered in the evaluation of all
patients with spinal pain.19 Failure to recognize the contributions of fear, anxiety,
depression, and other psychosocial stressors to pain and disability may lead to poor
outcomes.

Multidisciplinary Care
Multidisciplinary care refers to organized treatment programs that involve professionals
across multiple disciplines who working in a coordinated manner to provide
physical/exercise treatment; psychological treatment; and, potentially, other forms of
treatment, including vocational and work-specific training. The professionals involved in
this type of care vary by program but may include physicians (physical medicine,
rehabilitation, anesthesiology, surgery, others), physical therapists, occupational
therapists, psychologists, vocational specialists, exercise physiologists, and additional
providers. In patients with chronic spine pain, multidisciplinary treatment programs may
afford benefits with regard to pain, disability, quality of life, and work status.27,28
In general, multidisciplinary treatment programs are used to treat patients who have
substantial functional or vocational limitations associated with their pain. Often,
multidisciplinary treatment programs are founded on psychological principles of goal-
directed, quantified exercise programs and the minimization of adverse behaviors and
beliefs related to chronic pain. Variability in program design, availability in a community,
and relatively high costs affect the highly selective nature of multidisciplinary treatment
programs. Formal multidisciplinary programs are resource intensive and generally are
reserved for patients who are not progressing via more standard treatment approaches,
particularly those with considerable psychological contributors to their pain and
disability and/or complex return-to-work issues.

Interventional Spine Management
Epidural steroid injections are intended to manage radicular pain and are not indicated for the
management of axial LBP (Figure 4).
Medial branch blocks are performed as a diagnostic procedure to help determine the
appropriateness of radiofrequency ablation for specific facet joints in the cervical or lumbar
spine.
Pain relief with repeat intra-articular injections is the current standard for the diagnosis of
sacroiliac pain.
No high-quality evidence supports the use of intra-articular sacroiliac joint injections or
radiofrequency ablation to manage suspected sacroiliac joint pain.

Interventional Spine Management
Interventional spine procedures have been steadily increasing in frequency over the past
25 years (Resource 5). Interventional spine procedures, such as epidural injections and
radiofrequency ablation, are widely used in the management of spinal pain despite
limited evidence with regard to efficacy or ideal indications. Given the relatively limited
evidence supporting their use, interventional spine procedures are likely overutilized.
Evidence supports the use of lumbar epidural steroid injections to manage radicular
pain associated with a disk herniation; such injections may result in a short-term
reduction in pain and improvement in function.29 Very little high-quality evidence
supports the use of other interventional spine procedures. Epidural steroid injections
are less beneficial in the management of spinal stenosis. Epidural steroid injections in
the cervical spine are not well studied but may be beneficial in the management of
radicular pain associated with a disk herniation; however, cervical transforaminal
injections are associated with a higher risk for complications than other epidural
injections. Epidural steroid injections are not indicated for or effective in the
management of numbness, weakness, or other neurologic loss.
No reliable method is available to determine if a particular facet joint is symptomatic
based on imaging studies or physical examination findings. Medial branch blocks are
performed as a diagnostic procedure to help determine the appropriateness of
radiofrequency ablation for specific facet joints in the cervical or lumbar spine. No high-
quality evidence supports the use of intra-articular facet joint injections. Low-level
evidence shows that, in a small subset of patients, a moderate duration (≥6 months) of
pain relief may be associated with radiofrequency ablation of the cervical or lumbar
facet joints. Better results with higher degrees of pain relief are associated with dual
medial branch blocks (best outcomes associated with 100% relief of pain).30,31
Sacroiliac joint pain cannot be reliably diagnosed via a patient history and physical
examination. Approximately 20% to 30% of patients in whom sacroiliac joint pain is

injections is the current standard for the diagnosis of sacroiliac pain. Although intra-

evidence supports the use of intra-articular sacroiliac joint injections or radiofrequency
ablation to manage suspected sacroiliac joint pain.
In general, interventional spine procedures should be thought of as potential treatment
options in a multidimensional approach to spinal pain rather than curative procedures.
Substantial adverse events are associated with many interventional spine procedures.
These procedures should not be used in place of treatment approaches with more
supportive evidence, including concurrent exercise and behavioral treatment.
Psychosocial risk factors for poor outcomes also should be considered before
proceeding with management.
Summary
Most patients with symptoms related to the spine will improve with observation and
nonsurgical treatment, particularly those with axial complaints alone.
Risk factors for LBP include demographic, psychosocial, physical, and occupational variables.
Pain is best thought of as a biopsychosocial problem; following a purely biologic or anatomic
model for understanding spinal pain is inadequate and ineffective in many patients,
particularly those with chronic pain. The STarT Back Screening Tool may help stratify patients
with LBP by psychosocial risk.
Electrodiagnostic studies can be used to differentiate radiculopathy from myelopathy but do
not have a role in the evaluation of patients with axial pain.
No medication or combination of medications is associated with long-term benefits in patients
with LBP. Duloxetine may afford modest short-term benefits in patients with chronic LBP.
Opioid medications, if used judiciously, also may afford short-term benefits in patients with
chronic LBP.
Multidisciplinary treatment programs often are effective but also are resource and cost
intensive; therefore, they often are reserved for patients in whom more traditional treatment
